title: Unit economics narrative: token-first pricing playbook
content:
Purpose:
This doc is a working playbook for GTM, sales, and product to align on: why tokens as the primary metric, how to frame unit economics to customers, a simple tier structure and discounting guardrails, and short scripts for common objections. It’s intentionally pragmatic — for SDR/demo, AE negotiations, and product docs.

Audience:
- AEs and SDRs who need compact talking points
- Product marketing for website/FAQ copy
- Pricing ops for contract/discount guardrails

Executive summary (TL;DR):
- Token pricing maps cost to actual consumption (per-token units approximate compute + model work) and therefore aligns customer incentives with Redwood’s serving optimizations (batching, KV caching, quantization).
- Position tokens as the primary unit, with simple entry-level tiers and predictable step-up discounts for committed/annual usage.
- Use clear discount bands and bundling rules (no stacking of % across promos) to preserve margin while enabling scale deals.

Why tokens (short narrative for sales):
- Neutral, instrumentable unit: tokens are a single measurable unit that captures both short and long prompts consistently.
- Aligns cost with value: customers pay for what they use — a high-throughput summarizer costs less per result than a long-context generation because tokens are consumed differently.
- Supports surface-level differentiation: we can offer lower token price for lighter models (fast/cheap) and premium tokens for high-accuracy models.
- Incentivizes optimization: customers adopting batching, caching, and prompt engineering see immediate $/result improvements; this is a sales win (show savings %)

How tokens map to customer stories (examples sales can use):
- Chatbot (multi-turn): "Talk of the town" — tokens map to total user bytes (prompt + replies). Optimizations: short prompts + context windowing.
- Document processing (long inputs): tokens ~ input size; Redwood’s chunking + KV cache reduces reprocessed context.
- Embeddings: billed per embedding token-equivalent (converted to unit for simplicity).

Suggested tier structure (simple, sales-friendly):
- Pay-as-you-go (Starter): no commit, higher $/k tokens, ideal for dev and PoC.
  - Pricing example: $2.50 per 1k tokens (placeholder).
- Growth (monthly/1m–25m tokens): modest discount, predictable unit economics.
  - Example band: $1.80 per 1k tokens, with volume pricing kicking in at 5m.
- Scale (committed/annual): significant discount for 12-month commits + enterprise features (SLA, VPC).
  - Example band: $0.90–$1.20 per 1k tokens depending on model tier + reserved capacity uplift.
- Enterprise / Dedicated pricing: custom; includes reserved capacity, inbound training, and SSO/KMS integrations.

Important packaging notes (do not overcomplicate):
- Keep the public page to 3 tiers + enterprise. Use model families (fast/cheap vs high-quality) as add-on token categories.
- Avoid per-request or per-capability metrics publicly — use tokens as canonical metric and translate internally to per-call examples.
- Bundles: offer a small dev bundle (e.g., 10k tokens free/credit) and trial credits to reduce friction.

Discounting guardrails (for pricing ops and AEs):
- Discount tiers by commit volume only; one discount applicable per contract. No stacking of promotional credits + commit discount unless explicitly approved.
- Negotiation bands (suggested):
  - SMB (< $5k ARR): up to 20% off list on 12mo commit
  - Mid-market ($5k–$50k ARR): 20–35% off list with 12mo, min commitment and defined usage floors
  - Strategic enterprise (> $50k ARR): 30–50% off list + reserved capacity and product SLAs; higher discounts require cross-functional approval (finance + rev ops)
- Volume acceleration (mid-contract): if customer consistently exceeds banded volume, apply retroactive credit to align to new band for next billing period (standard process; require finance sign-off above $100k).

Competitive notes (quick):
- Competitor A: per-call pricing for endpoints — simpler but leads to mismatch for long-context tasks. Our advantage: tokens scale better for diverse jobs and let customers control cost via prompt engineering.
- Competitor B: subscription + add-on CPU/GPU hours—predictable but locks customers into overprovisioning; Redwood’s tokens + reserved capacity hybrid gives both predictability and efficiency.
- Competitor C: pay-per-1k-characters — opaque mapping to compute. Tokens are more standard in ML community and easier to instrument.

Objection handling (sales scripts):
- "Tokens sound complicated": "Totally — let’s map it to a typical workflow. For a one-message chat, here’s the median token count and cost. We’ll include a calculator to estimate monthly bill and show optimizations to reduce that number."
- "I’m worried about bill variability": "We offer committed packages with lower price per token, and reserved capacity for predictable spend. We can also set soft-usage alerts and hard budget caps."
- "Why not just one price per API call?": "Per-call pricing hides variance across jobs and pushes teams to buy bigger seats. Tokens let you only pay for what you use and reward engineering work that reduces unnecessary tokens."

Sales enablement artifacts to produce (prioritized):
- Token cost calculator (spreadsheet + embed on pricing page) — include examples: chat, summarize 1000-token doc, batch inference for 10k docs.
- One-page cheat sheet for AEs: quick reference mapping of common product calls to median tokens and cost.
- Demo scripts showing savings from caching and batching (before/after cost).

Metrics and success signals to monitor (GTM + product):
- Average $/active-user per month (derived from tokens consumed) — want to see fall over time as customers optimize.
- Conversion rate from free credits -> paid (track average starting tokens used)
- Percent of revenue from committed contracts vs pay-as-you-go
- Churn correlated with token-price spikes or heavy tail usage patterns

Legal / commercial constraints (notes for contracts):
- Define token measurement clearly in contract (what counts as token, rounding behavior, model variants).
- Specify billing cadence, reconciliation, and overage treatment for committed contracts.

Open questions / decisions needed (for leadership):
- Publicly list starter price or show ranges only? (tradeoff: conversion vs margin flexibility)
- Do we create separate token SKUs for embeddings vs text-gen or translate internally? (operational complexity vs clarity)
- Allow trial promos to stack with commits for first-year only?

Appendix: quick AE scripts (two-paragraph examples)
- Elevator (30s): "We bill you by tokens — think of tokens as the number of words the model processes. That means you only pay when the model works for you, and you can directly reduce costs with batching, caching, and shorter prompts. For customers doing high-volume document processing we offer committed plans with reserved capacity so you get predictability and lower unit prices."
- Discovery prompt (for demos): "How many user messages or documents do you process monthly? Let’s pick a representative job and I’ll run it through our calculator — you’ll see how much you’d pay both on pay-as-you-go and with a modest 12-month commit. We’ll also show common levers to cut costs without losing quality."

Notes to product & finance:
- We need an internal mapping table: typical API calls -> median tokens -> model category. Product to provide by 2026-01-31.
- Finance: confirm break-even token price per top 5 model families (requested: cost-per-1k tokens and margin target) by next pricing review.

Working doc annotations (links & refs):
- See Confluence: CONF-4321-token-econ for modeling assumptions.
- Related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/pricing-proposals/pull/73
- JIRA: JIRA-PLG-998 (pricing page implementation)

Recent edits / TODOs (short):
- [ ] Finalize public starter price vs range decision (owner: Maya)
- [ ] Ship AE cheat sheet + token calculator (owners: Priya, Ethan)
- [ ] Approvals for discounting bands with finance (owner: Liam)

Rough brainstormed language options (pick 1–2 for site and pitch):
- Option A (developer-friendly): "Pay for what you use — tokens are the unit that maps directly to compute. Start free, scale with commitments."
- Option B (business-friendly): "Predictable unit pricing + committed discounts: pay less per request as you scale."
- Option C (value-first): "Lower costs when your app gets smarter — optimizations like caching and batching reduce your per-result cost."

End of doc. This is a living Drive file — expected to evolve after AE feedback and finance review.
